summary: An older (tricyclic) antidepressant used for depression and for several pain and migraine conditions. It often causes drowsiness, dry mouth and constipation, and an overdose can seriously harm the heart.
description: Amitriptyline is a tricyclic antidepressant (TCA), first introduced in 1961. It raises the brain chemicals serotonin and norepinephrine, and it also blocks histamine and acetylcholine, which causes drowsiness, dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision and trouble peeing (anticholinergic effects). It is still a benchmark antidepressant and is widely used at lower doses for chronic pain and to prevent migraines. Because the gap between a helpful dose and a harmful one is small, an overdose can harm the heart, and these side effects add up, it is usually tried after other options for depression, especially in older adults.
patient_summary: Amitriptyline (often known by the old brand name Elavil) is an older antidepressant that can help with depression, chronic pain, migraines, and some gut or bladder pain conditions. It is usually taken at night because it can cause drowsiness and a dry mouth. At low doses it is often used more for pain and sleep, and at higher doses it is used for depression. It has important safety warnings: it can increase suicidal thoughts in some children, teens and young adults, can affect the heart (especially in overdose), and should not be taken with certain other medicines like MAOIs. Doses need to be started low and increased slowly under medical supervision.

primary.context: An alternative antidepressant; a long-standing tricyclic shown to work better than placebo

off_label.context: Low-dose TCA for chronic neuropathic pain (eg, diabetic neuropathy, postherpetic neuralgia)
Low doses to help prevent migraines in some people
Low-dose therapy for IBS-related pain and global symptoms
Low dose as an add-on for sleep and pain in fibromyalgia
Bladder pain syndrome; low-dose bedtime use

therapeutic_response.display: 1–2 weeks: Early antidepressant effects may start.; 4–6+ weeks: The full antidepressant effect is often seen.; Days to weeks: Pain and migraine benefits may begin at low doses.; 13–36 hours: How long it takes for half the dose to leave your body (half-life), so it can be taken once a day (often at bedtime).

common_adverse_effects.notes: Often helpful for sleep at night, but can cause morning grogginess or daytime sleepiness.

common_adverse_effects.effect: Dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, urinary hesitancy
common_adverse_effects.notes: These are typical for TCAs; increase fluids and fiber, and contact your clinician if urinary retention or severe constipation occurs.
May cause gradual weight gain; monitoring diet and weight is recommended.

common_adverse_effects.effect: Dizziness or feeling faint when standing up (a drop in blood pressure), lightheadedness
common_adverse_effects.notes: Can cause falls, especially in older adults; stand up slowly and use caution with driving.

common_adverse_effects.effect: Sweating, tremor, headache, nervousness or agitation

serious_risks.risk: Suicidal thoughts or behaviors (boxed warning) particularly in children, adolescents, and young adults.
Heart-rhythm and conduction changes (PR/QRS/QT prolongation, seen on an ECG), irregular heartbeat and sudden death, especially in overdose or in people with heart disease.
Acute myocardial infarction or stroke exacerbation in predisposed patients.
Severe poisoning from its drying effects: overheating, a stopped bowel, being unable to pee, and sudden confusion (delirium), especially in overdose or in older adults.
Low blood sodium (hyponatremia), which can cause confusion, headache or seizures, especially in older adults or when taken with water pills (diuretics).
Angle-closure glaucoma precipitation in susceptible patients.

A rare emergency with very high fever, rigid muscles and confusion (neuroleptic malignant syndrome), and serotonin syndrome (too much serotonin: agitation, fever, shaking, fast heartbeat — get urgent help), usually with interacting medicines.

safety.black_box_warning: Antidepressants, including amitriptyline, increased the risk of suicidal thoughts and behavior in children, teens and young adults in short-term studies. Anyone taking it should be watched closely for worsening mood or suicidal thoughts, especially in the first 1–2 months and after dose changes. Tell your prescriber or get help right away if this happens. Amitriptyline is not approved for children.

contraindications.contraindication: Hypersensitivity to amitriptyline or any component of the formulation
Use with or within 14 days of monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs)
Taking cisapride at the same time
Acute recovery phase following myocardial infarction
Severe liver problems, or confusion and brain changes caused by liver failure, according to many expert sources
Angle-closure glaucoma or untreated narrow-angle glaucoma (usually avoided, because the drying effects can make it worse)
Serious trouble peeing or a severely enlarged prostate (usually avoided, because the drying effects can make it worse)

precautions: Suicidality: Monitor for new or worsening depression, suicidality, or unusual behavior changes. Educate families/caregivers to observe closely and maintain communication with the prescriber.

Heart and overdose: the gap between a helpful dose and a harmful one is small. Even a fairly small overdose can cause life-threatening heart-rhythm problems, very low blood pressure and dangerous drowsiness. If you are at risk of suicide, your prescriber may give you only a small supply at a time.

Heart disease: used with great caution if you have heart-rhythm or conduction problems, a past heart attack, or serious heart disease; a heart tracing (ECG) before and during treatment is recommended if your risk is higher.

Dizziness and falls: it can make you dizzy or faint when standing up (a drop in blood pressure), which raises the risk of falls, especially in older adults. It is started at a low dose and raised slowly.
Drying effects: it can worsen constipation, trouble peeing, narrow-angle glaucoma, memory problems and sudden confusion (delirium), especially in older adults or people with dementia.
Seizures: it makes seizures more likely; used with caution if you have epilepsy, a brain injury, or take other medicines that make seizures more likely.

Serotonin syndrome: the risk goes up when combined with other medicines that raise serotonin (e.g., SSRIs, SNRIs, MAOIs, certain opioids, triptans). Too much serotonin can cause agitation, confusion, fever, shaking, muscle twitching and a fast heartbeat — get urgent help.

Bipolar disorder: it may trigger mania or hypomania in people with bipolar disorder. You should be checked for bipolar disorder before starting, and an antidepressant on its own should be avoided in bipolar depression.
Liver problems: the body clears it more slowly, so blood levels are higher; doses should be lowered, and it may not be suitable with severe liver disease.
Older adults: listed by the Beers and STOPP guides as a medicine older people should usually avoid, because of strong drying effects, dizziness when standing up and the risk of falls.

interactions.interactant: MAOIs (eg, phenelzine, tranylcypromine, selegiline, isocarboxazid, linezolid, methylene blue)
interactions.mechanism: High risk of serotonin syndrome and a dangerous spike in blood pressure.
interactions.action: Should not be used together; leave at least 14 days between stopping an MAOI and starting amitriptyline, and the other way round.

interactions.interactant: Other medicines that raise serotonin (SSRIs, SNRIs, triptans, tramadol, St. John’s wort, certain opioids)
interactions.action: Use with caution; monitor closely for serotonin toxicity.

interactions.interactant: Medicines that block the liver enzyme CYP2D6 (e.g., fluoxetine, paroxetine, bupropion, some antipsychotics)
interactions.mechanism: Increased amitriptyline and nortriptyline levels; greater side effects and QT risk.
interactions.action: Consider dose reductions of amitriptyline and monitor for toxicity.

interactions.mechanism: Additive risk of QT prolongation and malignant arrhythmias.
interactions.action: Avoid or use with ECG monitoring and correction of electrolytes.

interactions.mechanism: Enhanced CNS and respiratory depression, increased overdose risk.
interactions.action: Avoid combinations when possible; if used, use lowest effective doses and counsel about overdose danger.

interactions.interactant: Other medicines with strong drying effects (e.g., oxybutynin, some antipsychotics, antihistamines)
interactions.mechanism: Severe drying-effect poisoning: being unable to pee, a stopped bowel, sudden confusion and overheating.
interactions.action: Avoid or minimize use; monitor closely in high-risk patients.

interactions.mechanism: Potentiation of cardiovascular effects (tachycardia, hypertension, arrhythmias).
interactions.action: Monitor BP and heart rate; consider dose adjustments.

monitoring_requirements.parameter: Mood symptoms, suicidality, anxiety, agitation, and overall functioning (especially during first 1–2 months and after dose changes).
Heart rate, blood pressure and heart tracing (ECG) if you have heart disease, are older, or take higher doses
Blood salts, especially sodium, in older adults or anyone at risk of low blood sodium
Weight and BMI, metabolic parameters if clinically indicated.
Liver function tests if symptoms suggest hepatotoxicity (jaundice, dark urine, abdominal pain).
Signs of drying-effect poisoning: confusion, being unable to pee, severe constipation, vision changes
Blood levels of amitriptyline and nortriptyline in some cases (for example, suspected overdose, no benefit, or when the body handles it unusually)

special_populations.pregnancy: Tricyclics are not usually the first choice in pregnancy, but may be continued when the benefits clearly outweigh the risks, especially if they have worked before. Limited data do not show a clear link to major birth defects, but there are reports of temporary symptoms in newborns. Untreated depression also carries risks for the pregnancy and the baby, so decide together with your care team.
special_populations.lactation: Amitriptyline and nortriptyline appear in breast milk at low levels. Most reports suggest low risk, but rare cases of infant sedation have been described. Monitor infants for excessive sleepiness or poor feeding; consider alternative agents if starting a new antidepressant in a breastfeeding parent.
special_populations.pediatric: Not approved in children or teenagers for depression. Tricyclics are generally not tried first at this age because there is limited evidence that they work and there are safety concerns. If used for pain or other reasons, the dose must be carefully based on weight and closely checked.
special_populations.geriatric: Listed as a medicine older adults should usually avoid (Beers/STOPP) because of strong drying effects, dizziness when standing up, falls, and effects on thinking and memory. Other options are preferred when possible; if used, it is started very low, raised slowly, and closely watched.

pharmacokinetics.half_life: Approximately 13–36 hours (longer in older adults and hepatic impairment)
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Extensive hepatic metabolism (primarily CYP2D6; also CYP2C19 and others) to active metabolite nortriptyline and other metabolites
pharmacokinetics.excretion: Urine (mostly as metabolites; minimal unchanged drug); small amount via feces

dosing.titration: Dosing depends on indication, age, comorbidities, and sensitivity to anticholinergic and sedating effects. Lower doses are typically used for pain and migraine, while higher doses are reserved for depression under close supervision.

discontinuation.taper_guidance: If you have taken amitriptyline for 4 weeks or more, it should be lowered gradually over 2–4 weeks (or longer after high doses or long-term use) to reduce withdrawal symptoms (e.g., nausea, headache, trouble sleeping, irritability, flu-like symptoms, return of anxiety or depression). Longer tapers (3 months or more) may help after years of use or if you have had withdrawal symptoms before.

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Amitriptyline is approved for major depressive disorder in adults and is widely used off-label at lower doses for multiple chronic pain and headache conditions.
items: Treatment of {link:condition:major-depressive-disorder:major depressive disorder (unipolar)} in adults.
off_label: Chronic neuropathic pain (eg, diabetic neuropathy, postherpetic neuralgia).
Irritable bowel syndrome–associated pain and global symptoms.
sections.patient_text: Amitriptyline is approved for depression and is also commonly used in much lower doses to help with nerve pain, migraine prevention, and some chronic gut or bladder pain conditions.

sections.heading: What People Feel

quotes: It really knocked me out at night, which helped my sleep but made mornings rough.
At a low dose I finally slept through the night for the first time in years.
If I took it too late, I felt groggy well into the next day.
items.note: Sedation is dose-dependent and often helpful for insomnia, but can impair daytime functioning if excessive.

quotes: My mood slowly lifted over a few weeks—nothing dramatic, just less heavy.
My nerve pain eased up enough that I could get through the day.

sections.intro: Experiences vary with dose and indication, but common themes reported by patients include:

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Initial antidepressant effects typically appear within 1–2 weeks, with full benefits often requiring 4–6 weeks or longer. For pain and sleep indications, some benefit can occur within days to a couple of weeks. The elimination half-life is 13–36 hours, allowing once-daily dosing in many patients.
key_points: 1–2 weeks: Early antidepressant effects may emerge.
4–6+ weeks: Full antidepressant response is often seen.
Days to weeks: Pain and migraine benefits may begin at low doses.
13–36 hours: Elimination half-life, supporting once-daily dosing (often at bedtime).

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: A Cochrane meta-analysis found that amitriptyline was significantly more effective than placebo for acute treatment response in major depression. The odds of response with amitriptyline were approximately 2.7 times higher than with placebo (OR 2.67, 95% CI 2.21–3.23), corresponding to an estimated number needed to treat of 4–5. More patients discontinued due to adverse effects, reflecting substantial side-effect burden.
sections.clinical_details: Leucht and colleagues performed a Cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis of 39 randomized controlled trials comparing amitriptyline with placebo in adults with major depressive disorder. Eighteen studies (n=1,987) contributed to the primary response outcome, defined as a clinically significant improvement on standard depression rating scales. Amitriptyline showed superior efficacy to placebo (OR 2.67, 95% CI 2.21–3.23), with high overall response rates but increased discontinuation due to adverse events. The authors concluded that amitriptyline is an efficacious antidepressant but less favorable than many newer agents in terms of tolerability and safety, particularly in overdose.

citation.authors: Leucht C, Huhn M, Leucht S
citation.title: Amitriptyline versus placebo for major depressive disorder

sections.heading: Warnings & Precautions ⚠️
sections.black_box: Antidepressants, including amitriptyline, increased the risk of suicidal thoughts and behavior in children, teens and young adults in short-term studies. Anyone taking it should be watched closely for worsening mood or suicidal thoughts, especially in the first 1–2 months and after dose changes. Tell your prescriber or get help right away if this happens. Amitriptyline is not approved for children.
other: Suicidality: Monitor for new or worsening depression, suicidality, or unusual behavior changes. Educate families/caregivers to observe closely and maintain communication with the prescriber.

Cardiotoxicity and overdose: Amitriptyline has a narrow therapeutic index. Even relatively modest overdoses can cause life-threatening arrhythmias, hypotension, and CNS depression. Prescribe conservative quantities in patients at suicide risk.

Cardiac disease: use with great caution in people with conduction abnormalities, prior heart attack (MI), or significant cardiovascular disease; baseline and follow-up ECGs are recommended for people at higher risk.
Orthostatic hypotension and falls: Alpha-1 blocking and anticholinergic effects increase fall risk, particularly in older adults; start low and go slow.
Anticholinergic burden: May worsen constipation, urinary retention, narrow-angle glaucoma, cognitive impairment, and delirium, especially in older adults or those with dementia.
Seizure risk: lowers the seizure threshold; use cautiously in people with seizure disorders, brain injury, or other seizure-threshold–lowering medicines.

Serotonin syndrome: Risk increases when combined with other serotonergic agents (eg, SSRIs, SNRIs, MAOIs, certain opioids, triptans). Monitor for agitation, confusion, autonomic instability, clonus, and hyperreflexia.
Bipolar disorder: may trigger mania or hypomania in people with bipolar disorder; screen for bipolar disorder before starting and avoid an antidepressant on its own in bipolar depression.
Hepatic impairment: Reduced clearance and higher plasma concentrations; doses should be reduced and severe hepatic disease may contraindicate use.
Older adults: Identified by Beers and STOPP criteria as potentially inappropriate due to strong anticholinergic effects, orthostatic hypotension, and fall risk.
patient_counseling: Report any new or worsening sadness, irritability, agitation, or suicidal thoughts immediately, especially in the first weeks of treatment or after dose changes.
Avoid alcohol and be cautious with other medicines that cause drowsiness; these can dangerously increase sedation.
Rise slowly from sitting or lying positions to reduce dizziness and fainting.
Do not stop amitriptyline suddenly after several weeks or months of use; your doctor will usually taper the dose to reduce withdrawal symptoms.
Keep this medicine out of reach of children and others due to serious overdose risk.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Side effects are driven largely by strong anticholinergic, antihistaminic, and alpha-1 adrenergic blockade, with important cardiac and CNS risks at higher doses or in overdose.
plain_language_list: Drowsiness or feeling very sleepy, especially at first.
Dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, and difficulty urinating.
Weight gain and increased appetite over time.
Dizziness or lightheadedness, especially when standing up.
Sweating, tremor, headache, nervousness, or agitation.
Sexual side effects such as reduced libido or trouble with arousal.

common.patient_note: Often helpful for sleep at night, but can cause morning grogginess or daytime sleepiness.

common.symptom: Dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, urinary hesitancy
common.patient_note: These are typical for TCAs; increase fluids and fiber, and contact your clinician if urinary retention or severe constipation occurs.
May cause gradual weight gain; monitoring diet and weight is recommended.
Can cause falls, especially in older adults; stand up slowly and use caution with driving.

common.symptom: Sweating, tremor, headache, nervousness or agitation

serious: Suicidal thoughts or behaviors (boxed warning) particularly in children, adolescents, and young adults.
Cardiac conduction abnormalities (PR/QRS/QT prolongation), arrhythmias and sudden death, especially in overdose or in people with heart disease.
Acute myocardial infarction or stroke exacerbation in predisposed patients.
Severe anticholinergic toxicity (hyperthermia, ileus, urinary retention, delirium), particularly in overdose or in older adults.
Hyponatremia/SIADH, especially in older adults or with concomitant diuretics.
Angle-closure glaucoma precipitation in susceptible patients.
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome and serotonin syndrome (usually with interacting drugs).

sections.intro: Amitriptyline has important interactions through serotonergic mechanisms, CYP2D6 metabolism, anticholinergic burden, and cardiac conduction effects.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: If you have taken amitriptyline for 4 weeks or more, it should be lowered gradually over 2–4 weeks (or longer after high doses or long-term use) to reduce withdrawal symptoms (e.g., nausea, headache, insomnia, irritability, flu-like symptoms, return of anxiety or depression). Longer tapers (3 months or more) may help after years of use or if you have had withdrawal symptoms before.
sections.patient_text: Do not stop amitriptyline suddenly. Your doctor will usually lower the dose slowly over weeks or months to reduce the risk of withdrawal symptoms and relapse of depression or pain.

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Dosing depends on indication, age, comorbidities, and sensitivity to anticholinergic and sedating effects. Lower doses are typically used for pain and migraine, while higher doses are reserved for depression under close supervision.

adult.depression_initial: 25–50 mg/day as a single bedtime dose or in divided doses.
adult.depression_titration: Increase by 25–50 mg/day at intervals of ≥1 week based on response and tolerability.
adult.depression_usual: 100–300 mg/day in 1–3 divided doses (higher doses generally reserved for inpatients or closely supervised patients).
adult.chronic_pain_low_dose: 10–25 mg at bedtime; titrate by 10–25 mg every 1–2 weeks to usual range 25–75 mg/day (max 100–150 mg/day depending on indication and tolerability).
adult.migraine_prophylaxis: 10–25 mg at bedtime; may increase gradually to 50–100 mg/day based on response and side effects.
adult.notes: Start low and go slow, especially in older adults or patients sensitive to anticholinergic or sedating effects. Give higher total doses at bedtime when feasible to minimize daytime sedation.

sections.patient_text: For depression, the dose usually starts low (25–50 mg a day) and is increased slowly up to 100–300 mg a day if needed. For pain or migraines, much lower doses are used (often 10–25 mg at night, sometimes up to 50–75 mg). Your doctor will adjust the dose based on how you feel and what side effects you have.

renal_adjustments.dose: No formal adjustment typically needed; use with caution and start at the low end of the dose range.
renal_adjustments.patient_note: Kidney problems usually do not require changing the dose, but your doctor may be extra cautious and start low.

hepatic_adjustments.condition: Hepatic impairment (cirrhosis or chronic liver disease)
hepatic_adjustments.dose: Use lower initial doses (≈50% of usual) and titrate slowly; avoid in severe hepatic impairment or encephalopathy.
hepatic_adjustments.patient_note: If you have liver disease, you will usually start with a lower dose, and in severe liver disease this medicine may not be recommended.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Amitriptyline requires careful risk–benefit consideration in pregnancy, breastfeeding, pediatric, and geriatric populations.
sections.pregnancy: TCAs are not considered first-line in pregnancy but may be continued when benefits clearly outweigh risks, especially if previously effective. Limited data do not show a clear major malformation signal, but there are case reports of neonatal adaptation symptoms. Untreated depression also carries obstetric and neonatal risks; decisions should involve shared decision-making.
sections.lactation: Amitriptyline and nortriptyline appear in breast milk at low levels. Most reports suggest low risk, but rare cases of infant sedation have been described. Monitor infants for excessive sleepiness or poor feeding; consider alternative agents if starting a new antidepressant in a breastfeeding parent.
sections.pediatrics: Not FDA-approved in children or adolescents for depression; TCAs are generally avoided as first-line in this population due to limited efficacy data and safety concerns. If used for pain or other indications, dosing must be carefully weight-based and monitored.
sections.geriatrics: Listed as potentially inappropriate (Beers/STOPP) due to strong anticholinergic effects, orthostatic hypotension, falls, and cognitive effects. Prefer alternatives when possible; if used, start very low, titrate slowly, and monitor closely.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Mood symptoms, suicidality, anxiety, agitation, and overall functioning (especially during first 1–2 months and after dose changes).
Heart rate, blood pressure and ECG in people with cardiac disease, in older adults, or at higher doses.
Electrolytes (particularly sodium) in older adults or those at risk for SIADH/hyponatremia.
Weight and BMI, metabolic parameters if clinically indicated.
Liver function tests if symptoms suggest hepatotoxicity (jaundice, dark urine, abdominal pain).
Signs of anticholinergic toxicity (confusion, urinary retention, severe constipation, visual changes).
Serum amitriptyline/nortriptyline levels in selected cases (eg, toxicity, nonresponse, complex pharmacokinetics).

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Amitriptyline is available as generic oral tablets in multiple strengths, allowing flexible titration across antidepressant and low-dose pain regimens.
items: Oral tablets: 10 mg, 25 mg, 50 mg, 75 mg, 100 mg, 150 mg (strengths vary by market and manufacturer).

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Amitriptyline inhibits the reuptake of serotonin and norepinephrine into presynaptic neurons, increasing their levels in the synaptic cleft. It also has strong antihistaminic (H1-blocking), anticholinergic (muscarinic-blocking), and alpha-1 adrenergic–blocking properties. These additional receptor effects contribute to its sedative properties, weight gain, dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, orthostatic hypotension, and cardiac conduction effects. At lower doses it appears to modulate descending pain pathways in the central nervous system, which underlies its benefit in neuropathic pain and migraine prevention.

image.alt: Diagram showing amitriptyline blocking serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake and its anticholinergic/antihistamine effects.

sections.patient_text: Amitriptyline works by increasing certain brain chemicals (serotonin and norepinephrine) that affect mood and pain. It also blocks other receptors, which is why it can make you sleepy and give you a dry mouth or constipation.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: Amitriptyline is a highly efficacious but less well-tolerated antidepressant compared with many newer agents. For major depressive disorder, it is usually considered after SSRIs, SNRIs, and other first-line options, particularly in patients without significant cardiac disease and with low suicide risk. At low doses, it occupies a key role in the management of chronic neuropathic pain and migraine, often at doses below those used for depression. In older adults, amitriptyline is generally avoided due to anticholinergic and cardiovascular risks; if a TCA is needed, secondary amines such as nortriptyline may be better tolerated.

sections.heading: Clinical Pearls ✨
items: Highly efficacious for MDD vs placebo but less favored today due to anticholinergic burden, sedation, weight gain, and overdose lethality.
Low-dose (10–25 mg) bedtime regimens often provide meaningful benefit for chronic pain and migraine with a more tolerable side-effect profile than antidepressant-level doses.
Avoid in people with significant cardiac conduction disease or high suicide risk when safer alternatives are available.
In older adults, amitriptyline is usually avoided; nortriptyline or other agents may be better tolerated if a TCA is needed.
Therapeutic drug monitoring (combined amitriptyline + nortriptyline 80–200 ng/mL) can help optimize dosing or evaluate suspected toxicity.

sections.heading: Availability and Regulatory Status
sections.text: Amitriptyline is widely available as a generic oral tablet in multiple strengths in the US, Canada, and many other countries. The Elavil brand is discontinued in some markets but the molecule remains commonly prescribed, particularly for off-label pain and migraine indications.

faqs.a: Amitriptyline is an older antidepressant used to treat major depressive disorder in adults. At lower doses it is also commonly prescribed for chronic nerve pain, migraine prevention, and certain chronic gut or bladder pain conditions.

faqs.q: How long does it take for amitriptyline to work?
faqs.a: For depression, some improvement may be noticed within 1 to 2 weeks, but full benefits usually take 4 to 6 weeks or longer. For pain or migraine prevention, some improvement can appear within days to a few weeks, with best effects often after several weeks at a stable dose.

faqs.q: Is amitriptyline safe for older adults?
faqs.a: Amitriptyline is generally not preferred for adults 65 and older, because its strong drying and sedating effects raise the risk of falls, confusion and constipation. When an antidepressant or pain medicine is needed in older adults, safer options are usually chosen first.

faqs.q: Can I drink alcohol while taking amitriptyline?
faqs.a: Alcohol can significantly increase the drowsiness and coordination problems caused by amitriptyline and makes overdose more dangerous. It is best to avoid or strictly limit alcohol use while taking this medication.

faqs.q: Can I stop taking amitriptyline abruptly?
faqs.a: Stopping amitriptyline suddenly can cause withdrawal symptoms such as nausea, headache, sleep problems, irritability, and return of depression or pain. The dose should be reduced gradually under your clinician’s supervision.
